vignette: Ali, a 40-year-old married Middle Eastern software engineer, has been struggling with the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster that occurred last year. The traumatic event was a powerful earthquake that struck unexpectedly during one of his weekly team meetings at work. As the building shook violently and people screamed in terror, Ali found himself trapped under debris for hours before he was rescued. Since then, every unexpected movement around him triggers intense fear responses, as if the ground could shift again without warning. Ali's marriage has taken a significant hit because of his newfound hypervigilance. He now constantly monitors his surroundings and identifies escape routes wherever he goes. This behavior is particularly evident at work, where he feels anxious in crowded spaces. Whenever someone approaches him unexpectedly, whether it’s a colleague or even his own wife at home, he reacts with alarm and sometimes physical recoil. The memories of the earthquake are vivid and terrifying. He often hears the sounds from that day—the screams, the crashing debris—as if they were happening again. The fragmented nature of these recollections makes it difficult for him to put them in order, leaving him feeling disoriented and trapped in a cycle of fear. Ali believes he cannot escape the memories; when triggered, he experiences full sensory reliving of the event, which leaves him breathless and drenched in sweat. Ali’s negative appraisals have deepened his sense of threat and led to a pervasive belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore. He is haunted by thoughts that if someone else had been there instead of him, they wouldn’t have ended up trapped and terrified like he did. This self-comparison fuels his despair and reinforces his feeling of being cursed with misfortune. To cope with the relentless intrusions of these memories, Ali has adopted maladaptive strategies such as forcing himself to think only positive thoughts. However, this rigid positivity is often overshadowed by ruminations about how to get even with those he believes were responsible for his suffering. His attempts at reframing have led him to avoid medical cues like hospitals and physical examinations, adding another layer of stress to an already overwhelmed psyche. The cycle intensifies as Ali’s threat perception grows stronger. Each trigger—from the sudden movement in a crowded room to the touch of a colleague—sparks intense fear responses that fuel his sense of vulnerability. These heightened states often lead him back into his maladaptive strategies, where he retreats into forced positivity and rumination. Over time, this loop has led to significant changes in how Ali interacts with the world. His avoidance behaviors have strained his relationships at work and home. Colleagues note that he is distant and preoccupied, and his wife feels alienated by his constant need for reassurance and control over their environment. What finally brought Ali to seek help was a recent incident where he had an intense panic attack in the office after hearing loud construction noises outside. The episode left him feeling isolated and desperate for relief from the relentless cycle of fear and negativity. Ali is most afraid that these symptoms will only worsen, but he also hopes to reclaim some semblance of the happy person he used to be before the earthquake shattered his sense of security and well-being.
